title: Berkshire Hathaway Raises Delta Air Lines Stake to $5 Billion in Renewed Aviation Bet
excerpt: Warren Buffett's conglomerate boosted its Delta position by 40% in the second quarter, deepening a comeback to an industry it famously abandoned during the pandemic.
body:
• Berkshire Hathaway increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 40% in Q2 2026 to 57 million shares worth approximately $5 billion, adding roughly $1.5 billion in the quarter.
  • The move follows Berkshire's initial $2.65 billion Delta investment in Q1 2026 — its first airline stake since selling all four airline positions at a loss during the pandemic in April 2020.
  • Berkshire also boosted its Alphabet stake by 80% to 106 million shares worth $36 billion, while trimming its Bank of America position by 30 million shares.
  • The portfolio moves reflect new CEO Greg Abel's increasing influence, though Buffett remains involved in major investment decisions as chairman.

Berkshire Hathaway is doubling down on its return to airlines. The conglomerate increased its stake in Delta Air Lines by about 40% during the second quarter to 57 million shares, a holding now worth approximately $5 billion, according to its latest 13-F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Delta purchases in the quarter totaled roughly $1.5 billion, according to Barron's estimates, making it Berkshire's second-largest equity purchase of the period behind Alphabet.

The Comeback Bet

The expanded Delta position deepens a comeback that stunned longtime Berkshire watchers. In Q1 2026, Berkshire disclosed a brand-new $2.65 billion stake in the airline — 39.8 million shares — its first foray into aviation since Warren Buffett sold stakes in Delta, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines in April 2020, early in the pandemic.

"The world had changed" for aviation, Buffett said at the time. He had long been skeptical of airlines as investments, once quipping that a far-sighted capitalist should have shot down Orville Wright's plane at Kitty Hawk. "It turned out I was wrong," he later acknowledged of the pandemic exit, calling it an "understandable mistake."

"The worst sort of business is one that grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money. Think airlines."

— Warren Buffett, 2007 Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder Letter

Abel's Imprint

The Delta investment carries Greg Abel's fingerprints. Abel succeeded Buffett as CEO at the end of 2025 after six decades of Buffett's leadership. He took over management of 94% of Berkshire's stock holdings, with investment manager Ted Weschler handling the remaining 6%.

Delta is widely regarded as among the best-run large U.S. airlines, and Abel's bet signals confidence in the carrier's premium business model and improved balance sheet. But Berkshire didn't exactly buy at a bargain — Delta's stock is up 66% over the past five years, and the airline faces headwinds from rising fuel prices and potential economic slowdown.

Alphabet Surge, Bank of America Trim

Delta wasn't the only notable move. Berkshire's Alphabet stake surged roughly 80% in the quarter to 106 million shares, reflecting a direct purchase from Alphabet in June combined with open-market buys. The position is now worth about $36 billion, placing it in a rough tie with Coca-Cola as Berkshire's third-largest equity holding behind Apple and American Express.

Berkshire's Alphabet purchases likely totaled about $16 billion, accounting for most of its $23 billion in stock purchases during the quarter.

On the selling side, Berkshire trimmed its sizable Bank of America stake by 30 million shares to 483 million shares, now worth about $31 billion. It also reduced positions in Kroger, Capital One Financial, Nucor, and Ally Financial.

A $350 Billion Portfolio in Transition

Berkshire's equity portfolio now exceeds $350 billion. Apple remains the largest holding at 227.9 million shares — unchanged from the prior quarter after three consecutive quarters of cuts. The Q2 filing showed no consequential new equity positions, marking a rare three months without a major new investment.

The Alphabet and Bank of America moves were likely orchestrated by Buffett, who remains chairman and involved in investment decisions. The smaller-stock activity, including Delta and the additions to Macy's, Lennar, and New York Times, probably came from Weschler, who manages about $20 billion of the portfolio.

What's Next

With nearly $5 billion now committed to Delta and a rapidly growing Alphabet position, Berkshire under Abel's leadership is staking out new territory while maintaining the high-conviction, low-turnover approach that defined the Buffett era. Whether Delta can deliver the kind of long-term returns Berkshire demands will test whether today's airline industry is truly a different animal from the one Buffett once called the worst sort of business.
